utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness is protected witness K58 via videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this is a witness whose evidence will be delivered by video conference link?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. She's being submitted under paragraphs 25 through 32, 72(l), 76, and 77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Can we have the witness now, please. Good morning, Madam, can you hear me? Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document now being placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness cannot be heard properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Two things arise. Thank you for taking the solemn declaration. Please be seated. The interpreter had some difficulty hearing what was said there, so I would be grateful if the registrar would adjust the microphone. And I assume that the witness is wearing headphones, which were not obvious on the photograph we have. TECHNICIAN: [Pristina] Your Honour, the witness is listening on loud-speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Witness K58, can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could the interpreter hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter couldn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, yes, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm afraid we'll have to try to adjust that microphone, Mr. Haider, to make it a bit easier so the witness doesn't have to keep bending down to speak. Even if a book was placed under it, it would make a difference. Thank you very much. We can now continue, Witness K58, with your evidence and the first person to ask you some questions will be on behalf of the Prosecution and that will be Ms. Carter. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to direct the witness to P2477, which is the witness identification sheet, and I also have a hard copy for the Court's use. This is not to be displayed on e-court because it will be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ms. K58, I'm showing you the witness identification sheet. Can you please review it and confirm that that is, in fact, your name and place of birth; however, it is my understanding that the date of birth is inaccurate. And it should be the date of birth that is reflected on your 92 bis presiding officer attestation. Can you review that information and confirm that it is in fact correct without reading it out before to the Court.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: The first time, the date of birth was not correct, because my date of birth was incorrect. The second time, everything is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At this time I would tender P2477 under seal with the caveat that the date of birth is inaccurate and that the date of birth reflected in the attestation should be the one for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ms. K58, as we discussed during proofing, the Court already has your statement, and I'm just going to ask you a few questions in regards to clarifications within the statement. I first want to direct you to when you were driven out of your village and you indicate you were driven out for six months. Is this six months prior to March 26th, 1999, or are you referring to a deportation on March 26th, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll object to the use of the word "deportation." She's trying to get this witness to give legal conclusions, which I think is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, you should, I think, rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you indicate in your statement that you were driven out of your village and were forced to stay in Drenoc for six months. Was this six-month period prior to 26 March of 1999, or are you referring to being driven out and forced to stay in Drenoc on the 26th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: The war started six months ago, and we were forced to go from our village to Drenoc village.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you say the war started six months ago, are you referring to 1998 or are you stating in the beginning in 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: It started at the beginning of 1999. I can't remember very well, but I know that I left my village and stayed in Drenoc for six months.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In paragraph 9 of your statement, beginning on page 3 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S, you indicate that some police officers entered Naim's house. Can you please describe those police officers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Yes. We were staying at the house of Naim Vishaj. The policemen came there and entered the house. They were dressed in police uniforms and asked us to leave the house by killing people and my maltreating people. They killed Daut Alickaj on the spot and Nezir Vishaj; and then they took Naim to a stable, I don't know, but we heard the shots being fired at him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, I need to stop you for just a moment, and I need you to back up. I need an answer to my original question. Can you please describe what the police looked like when they entered Naim's home.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: They were wearing police uniform. The first time they entered at 9.00 and called the landlord, the owner of the house, and asked him who it was inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you said they were wearing police uniforms, what colour were those uniforms, and did they have a pattern or were they solid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: When they entered that day, they had on police clothes; then afterwards, there were forces dressed in two kinds of uniforms, police and camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: What did the police uniforms look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: The police uniforms were one solid colour, like greyish colour. The usual uniforms police wore. They had written on their arms "police" in Serbian, in Cyrillic letters.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I want you to look around yourself there in the videolink room. Is there anything that is approximately the colour that you saw the police wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: It is the greyish police uniform; the one that police used to wear in the past. How can I explain to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Outside of the uniforms, what kind of arms were they carrying, if any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: They had arms. They had rifles and machine-guns. I don't know what name it has.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated that later - and I believe you're referencing pages 3 and 4 in the English statement, as well as page 3 in the B/C/S statement - that an additional group entered some time later. What were these what you describe as paramilitaries, what did they look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Yes. The people of the other group had caps on, and they had camouflage-like green, grass green uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Did these paramilitaries have the same types of guns as the police, or did they have different types?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: They had other weapons. They had tanks. The tank was there when they forced us to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter couldn't hear the last part.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat, please, the last part of that answer. You said they had a tank, and then we could not hear what you said after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They were dressed in green uniform. They had the tank. They were on the tank, and we were surrounded -- we were around the tank. The tank was standing in the middle, and they were carrying long weapons on their shoulders, different kind of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, before you move on or move off that page, that and the previous page have a number of redactions in the copy of the statement I have. All the place names have been deleted. I take it there is a copy with all the place names in it?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The copy that I'm looking at has no redactions to it. It does appear in the -- I can tender my copy -- well, no, it's actually highlighted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It can be remedied later, but it is just to be sure that this isn't a gap you intend to fill in by oral question and answer. It can be dealt with later.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. When that correction is made, it will come in at K0482420, which is an unredacted copy of this witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, on page 4 of the English statement and page 4 of the Albanian statement and page 3 of the B/C/S, you indicated that when these people were forcing you from the home, they began beating the people who could not walk. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: When they drove us out of Naim's house, there were about 40, 50 of us; men, women, children, elderly people, paralyzed people. They didn't give us time even to wear our shoes. When a paralyzed woman of Nezir Vishaj, she could not walk. She could only drag herself. Her daughters were helping her, and the police were kicking at her, telling her to walk on. Her daughters told the policemen that she cannot walk, and they were just prodding her to walk on.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You later describe a removal of some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that leaves me now wondering what -- is that what beaten up means, as you understand that answer, just prodding her to make her walk?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you indicate that she was being -- the paralyzed woman was being prodded to walk, can you please describe exactly what was happening to her at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: She couldn't walk. They rallied us in one place. The policemen were behind us. But that woman was an elderly and paralyzed woman, and she wouldn't keep pace with us. So her daughters carried her, and that was a reason why the policemen beat her, because she couldn't walk.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you said they beat her, were they using their hands? Were they using any sort of weapon? What were they doing when they were beating this woman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: They had a stick, and they beat her with a stick on her back, telling her to walk on, walk on; and the daughters told, "She's paralyzed, she cannot."

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Later on at some point you indicate that some of the young girls were being removed in the middle of the night, and you had suspected some of them had been raped. Can you please describe for me what those young girls looked like when they came back in the room after being taken out by the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: This is a fact. I saw it with my own eyes. We were all in a room, 50, 60 people, and the policemen came in around midnight. I cannot tell you the exact time because there was no electricity, and we didn't even dare look at them. And they used the torch light and they said, "You, you, you come with us to clean," and they took them away.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You just indicated it was policemen who were coming in to take the girls out of the room. Was it the police who were describing in regular police uniforms, or was it the paramilitaries who you described to be in green camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: They were regular police; those who took away the girls.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Earlier on the witness said: It was darkness; there was no light. We couldn't see well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicated when these young girls came back -- excuse me, can you describe for me when they came back, did it appear that they were cleaning something, or did it seem that something else had happened to these young girls?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: No. They looked as if something had happened to them. They came crying with their hair disheveled, and one of the girls was behind me. I heard her talking with her mother. The mother asked her, "What did they do to you?" And she answered, "Mom, they raped us." This is what happened to us. I -- this I heard with my own ears, because she was standing behind my back.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: The next morning you indicate within your statement that some policemen had come in and given back some jewellery. Were these the same people who'd come in and taken the girls from the night before, or were these different people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, we were afraid. I couldn't look at their faces. The only thing I knew it is that they were policemen, but I can't say to you whether they were the same policemen. I was afraid. I had my seven children, and I was very much scared. But I can't ascertain that they were the same policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In your statement you list your husband, in addition to many other men, as being missing at the time that this statement was taken. Have you ever learned the fate of your husband or of those other men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: From the day they took them away, when we were kept hostage all day and night, and when they sent us to Albania around 9.00 or 10.00, to this day I know nothing of my husband and of the 64 other disappeared men.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You said after the time --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: And that day, all night they maltreated them, tortured them. And they send -- they gave back to us and they sent back to us some elderly people with broken ribs, who recounted to us everything that had happened to them during the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You had indicated also that after the men were moved from you, that the next day you were taken out of that village and followed a certain path to Kukes. On that path, were you escorted, or were you going on your own volition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: We were escorted by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Who were you escorted by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Within your statement, you indicate that paramilitaries were involved over this time-period. What were the paramilitaries doing from the 26th of March through the 29th of March?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: From the 26th of March to the 29th of March, in cooperation with the police, the paramilitaries took us, beat us, maltreated us, killed us, plundered us of our possessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: You indicate "in cooperation with the police." At the time the police were doing these actions, were the paramilitaries working in the same groups, or were they acting in two separate groups; the police doing things at one time and the paramilitaries doing the same things at another time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: They acted together; someone did one thing, the other did another thing. But I know that they cooperated together.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you have before you your witness statement, as well as the 92 bis attestation. This is the same document in which you reviewed during the proofing session. Outside of your date of birth, are you confirming that the information within that statement is true and correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Everything is correct, with the exception of my birth date, which was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Are you asking this Court to adopt this statement as your true and correct testimony; and that if you were asked all of these questions here in open court, you would give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Whatever I told you happened to me, and I don't know anything else other than what I have told you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender P2473, the 92 bis package of Witness K58; and for the record, apparently the e-courted statement is a full statement and does not contain the redactions that the Court was indicating previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And at this time I would pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness K78 [sic]. I have a number of questions for you, and I should be grateful if you will do your best to answer them as clearly as possible. In describing the events between the 26th and 29th of March, you say that on the 28th of March, the village of Beleg and the surrounding villages were shelled continuously. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. The village was shelled non-stop, and we went to take shelter at Naim Vishaj's house, where we stayed about two or three days until the police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just stop there, please. You've said it was shelled non-stop. That I understand as a concept. Can you say over what length of time that took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It went on all the time during the day and during the night. They didn't stop for one hour or even half an hour, so much so that we couldn't leave the house because we were afraid some shells might hit us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What damage did this do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The shells fell everywhere. They destroyed houses. They might have even killed people, who knows? I know that they shelled all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell us the identity of any house that was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, we didn't dare leave the houses, go even up to the yard. So I cannot tell you which house was hit. We only stayed there in the stonehouse, in Naim's house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you say that men were separated from women and children, and you also --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you also describe the men as being taken in small groups and coming back in -- some in their underwear; and you then say that Mehmet Mazrekaj was separated from the men and beaten up. Now, was he one of the -- was he --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just let me finish the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were returned, stripped of their clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was he one of the 66 men who were taken away and have not been seen again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Mehmet was lucky to have his tractor with him, and he managed to escape. Those persons who had with them their tractors managed to leave, go to Albania.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On page 3 in the English version of your statement you say that the policemen -- or the police ordered Naim Vishaj to take all men out. They lined them up. The door was opened, and then you say: "After the policemen let all the men in, they left Naim's house." Can you explain what happened there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. The policemen entered and told us -- Naim, "Who is inside?" Naim told them that, "I have refugees from Beleg and Drenoc." Then the policemen asked him to bring out all the men. Naim went into the room and asked all the men to go out into the yard. I ran because I heard what Naim was talking with the police, and I told my husband to tell Naim that he was from Drenoc for Naim not to have problems with the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How many men were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Approximately 15 men. Approximately, I would say ten, 15. To tell you the truth, I couldn't count them, but I would say about 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Later when you describe what happened to women, including yourself, and what happened to the young girls, you say that they were taken to the basement to be checked. And then you say later -- you refer later to the policemen or paramilitaries who checked us. What do you mean by "who checked us?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They -- all the population that was in the village was asked to go to large meadow and gather there. After that, they -- all the women -- first they lined -- checked the males, then the females. They took us in that -- to that basement and checked us one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can -- well, that's what I'd like you to explain. What do you mean by "checked us?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They searched us bodily. Some of us they even asked to take off the clothes because they wanted to see if we had money on us, because some of us did have money on the bodies; and when they found some money on some women or men, they beat them up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. O'Sullivan -- oh, sorry, just one moment. There is something we wish to discuss briefly, if you give us a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order will be: General Lukic, General Pavkovic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Milutinovic, General Lazarevic, and General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, witness K58, a number of other counsel representing the accused in the dock here will ask some questions; and the first counsel to question you will be on behalf of Mr. Lukic, and that is Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, ma'am. My name is Dan Ivetic, as you've heard, and I'm going to be asking you some questions. So please pay close attention to what I ask you and try to limit your responses to answers to those questions. Now, first of all, do you speak or read the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to the events in Beleg, you've just told us that it was actually the police that came to get the groups of girls and take them out of where you were in the meadow. Now, in your statement at page 6 of the English, you specifically identify that it was Mushk Jakupi's son who would come and pick up the girls. And you've mentioned two paramilitaries who came with a torch. Now, are you changing your testimony, or is it still your testimony that Mushk Jakupi came to pick out young girls from your room in Beleg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I do not change. The truth is that the police came with two paramilitaries. They took the girls away. I saw it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So how many total people came to take the girls away in Beleg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: How many people came? That is what you asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: One or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you had just --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: They came with a torch, and they looked at the girls with a torch.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. I'm trying to understand the testimony that you just gave when you said at line 21 of the transcript and 22 of the transcript,"The truth is the police came with two paramilitaries." Now, in your statement you have identified two paramilitaries who came with the torch and took four young girls first; and then you later identified that Mushk Jakupi's son was the one who would come and pick up the young girls in our room. Now, I'm trying to figure out how is it that the police figure into your testimony, since they are not referenced in your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: No, this is not true. It is not true that I mentioned Mushk Jakupi. I didn't recognise Jakupi. I saw police with paramilitaries. We couldn't recognise them,, we couldn't look to see who they were. I haven't mentioned Jakupi or his son. It was very dark. We could not see them. We were simply very, very scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that the situation was that it was very dark, but what I'm trying to make --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I've mentioned only the police in my declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I would actually have to question you then on that. You testified that you reviewed this statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor, and that it was accurate and correct in every regard. Now, I'm reading for you what your statement says. And it says at page 6, the middle of the page: "Mushk Jakupi's son was the one who would come and pick up young girls in our room." And previously you had identified Mushk Jakupi as being short, black hair, round face, normal build, around 30 years old. He was wearing green camouflage uniform. So I would ask you then: Is it correct that in addition to the two paramilitaries with the torch, Mushk Jakupi in a green uniform were the ones coming to pick up the girls?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: It was very dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall having a proofing session with the Office of the Prosecutor on the 10th of October, 2006?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And at the proofing session, wherein Ms. Carter asked you questions, you stated - and now I'm quoting - "while the paramilitaries were the ones soliciting the girls, the following day the police were still in the village." Why is it that your statement and the notes from your proofing session identify paramilitaries as being the ones who took the girls, and today you have changed your testimony to say it was the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Both sides were cooperating. Police, they were cooperating. I couldn't see them. I couldn't see them. I saw seven children who were surrounded. I couldn't see them in the eye. I couldn't see who were they. They came in and took the girls away; I saw this with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, I'm trying to find out how many persons came to take the girls. You earlier said one or two, and now you said that they were working together. I can't see how there can be a gentleman in a green uniform, one or two other people, and for it to cover as many organisations as you claim it covers, for there to be police involved as well. How many men with torches or without torches came to pick up the girls from your room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: One was standing at the front door. The other one went in with a torch and was looking at the girls who were beaten, and they took the girls away by the arms. We could not raise our eyes to see who they were; we were very afraid. However, I know that they entered, they came in, and they took the girls away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to these two individuals, did they have on the same uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: It was very dark. It was very dark, the middle of the night. We could not raise our eyes to see them. We could not see what uniform, how they were dressed. They were dressed -- this is what I know. I don't know who they were. It was very dark. I've forgotten also. At the moment, I would have been able to tell you, but now since then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I -- according to the transcript you just: "We could not see what uniform, how they were dressed." Is it your testimony you do not really know what uniform these men were wearing who came to take the young girls?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: No. They were police. They were wearing police uniforms. They were policemen. They had police uniform. They had the Serbian Croatian word on the arm that they were police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, you previously testified in my first question that you neither speak nor read Serbian, so how is it you knew they had the Serbian Croatian word on the arm for police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I have eight-year education. We know some Serbian language. I know some Cyrillic words. I can discern them. I cannot understand, and I cannot speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd like to ask you a couple of other things before we get to Beleg. I'd like to try and do things in a chronological order. Now, in your statement you mention that in your home town of Glodjane, there was an UCK headquarters. Now, what I need to know is with respect to your husband or any of his relatives in Glodjane or the surrounding area, were any of them members of the UCK in any manner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: No. My husband had seven children; he could not join UCK. We had -- our children were all little, from six months to 12 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. What about any relatives of your husband, were they UCK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: There were some from the village; however, I don't know on the whole village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Were your husband's relatives who were members of the UCK, were they from Glodjane or from Rastovice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: They were some from the village, but I don't know. There were no relative of my husband who were UCK.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, again I'm going to have to ask you to clear something up for me then. The supplemental information sheet I received from the Prosecutor's office, arising from your 10 October 2006 interview with them, says in paragraph 1: "Some of her husband's relatives were members of the KLA, but he was not, as he was the father of seven." Which is correct? Were members of your husband's family, his relatives, members of the UCK or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: My husband was not. I have seven children. Probably from the village or from the -- relatives -- who they were or who they were not, I don't know. I was simply staying at the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I still have to clarify. Were there relatives of your husband that you knew to be UCK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Not very close relatives, distant relatives; very, very close relatives, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could just briefly go into closed session so that I can check one name, and then we can go -- return back to open session. I intend to ask one name of someone who may or may not be a relative, and I don't want to reveal this witness's identity in doing so because the name is the same last name as the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's private session that's sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Private session should be sufficient, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right, ma'am, I'd like to move on now just to finish up with Glodjane. I'd like to ask you about this -- about the UCK presence in Glodjane. Do you know, if you know, approximately how many UCK members or fighters were in Glodjane, during the time you were there, obviously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I did not have anything to do with that. I'm sorry. I am not informed. I am a housewife, and our custom is to stay at home, not to deal with men's work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you hear or know about an individual named Ramush Haradinaj in Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I have heard this name. He lives at the other end of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was the head of the UCK in Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Chairman of the UCK in Gllojgan? I've heard about it, but I don't know anything more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair enough. Thank you. Now, in tending to your daily affairs in Glodjane, did you have occasion to see any of the UCK members; and if so, did they always wear military clothes, or did they also wear civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: We have not seen them. I am housewife. I never come out of the house. It's not in our tradition to come out of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now, you say in your statement that you left Glodjane because the Serb forces were positioning themselves in the village. Now, am I correct that at the time you left Glodjane, the Serb forces were actually engaged in armed combat with the UCK that were in and around the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: It was a fight. Due to the dangers, we left the place together with my husband and my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to focus just briefly on your stay in Drenovac, the six months that you were there. During that six-month time-period, did you come to be familiar with the UCK base in that village, headed by Dukaj Halil?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry, no. We had no opportunity to get some information. We were with little children. We did not know who UCK were fighting, why were UCK fighting and where were Serbia fighting. We were simply looking after our children.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, please clarify something for me. It's page 2 of 8 of the witness's English statement, the second-last line. What is the village referred to in the second-last line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can ask the witness or I can tell you that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just tell me what it says in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mine says Drenoc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've got a blank --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's Drenoc, which I believe is one of the of spellings Drenovac. It's also spelled as Drenofc with an fc. I believe it is the same is the village that our other witness, Mr. Mazrekaj, was from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you go up one paragraph, what is the village referred to in the previous paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It says, "We fled the village of Drenoc;" again, the same village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when you asked a question about leaving Glodjane, you're talking about 1998, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe so, yes, if we take the six months and extrapolate backwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I think the witness has just helped us clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, during your stay in Drenoc or Drenovac, did you become familiar with any Serb civilians living there who also fled in March of 1999, particularly in the adjacent hamlet of Locane?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I really don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's fair enough. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Because Drenoc is quite far from Lloqan.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now you say that the Serb forces came into Drenovac on March the 26th, 1999. Are you positive about that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: They came to the village, and they told the men from the village to leave; then the entire village gathered, women, children, everyone, and we left the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be helpful if you try and deal with the question that's being asked. The question is about a date. You've given a date for the police forces entering the village. Are you sure of that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm certain about the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, it is written 26th. I could have even forgotten. I don't know. I mean, it's been eight years now, and we've been through a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, am I correct that when the Serb forces came to Drenovac, that they were engaged in combat with the UCK in the surrounding area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I know that the police entered Drenoc, and they told the men - I don't know who exactly from the village - but they told the men to leave Drenoc. The whole village then left. When we left and arrived in Beleg village, some houses from Drenoc were on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you say -- thank you. You say that the whole village then left. Do you know how many persons there were in Drenovac that left on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but there were many of us, about 100. I know that we -- there were many of us, and we left the village, some on tractors and some on whatever they had, just to leave as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your statement you describe that when you came to Beleg, there was what you called heavy shooting - described at page 3 - that lasted all day long. Now, is it your understanding that there was a battle going on between the Serb forces and the UCK at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I don't know that. We didn't see the battles between the Serbs and the KLA, but I can tell you that there was heavy shooting, uninterrupted shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, when you went from Drenoc to Beleg, did you go through Prilep and the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: We passed through Prilep and then we took a road, which I was not familiar with, and that road took us to Beleg.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you pass by any police or UCK positions in the region that you passed through, between Drenoc and Beleg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, again, during the time-period you were in Beleg, first of all, are you familiar with the village of Pozar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I've heard of this village, but I don't know much about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the time-period when you were in Beleg, which I believe is between the 26th and the 28th or 29th of March, 1999, did you hear or come to know about any fierce fighting in the village of Pozar, specifically on the 27th, 28th, and 29th of March, between the UCK and the Serbs that resulted in two killed policemen and 15 wounded policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I really had no way how to get this information. We were in a house. We couldn't even dare go outside in the courtyard. There was no way I could learn about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And would it be a fact then that you would --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: And there was no one to inform us either. We could only hear the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, am I correct --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: The entire population was civilian, unarmed. They were defending themselves, protecting their own families, children, the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, now I'm confused. You said you didn't have anyone to inform you as to what was happening in Pozar, but now you tell me that the entire population was civilian, unarmed; that they were defending themselves. Did you in fact have information on what was going on in Pozar at the time, with respect to any armed struggles in that village or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: No, because we were blocked. We were there in Naim Vishaj's house. We were all civilians. We were protecting our own families, and there was no way we could get any information about what was going on. We were children, women, elderly there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So when you said the entire population was civilian, unarmed, you're talking about yourselves, not the persons in Pozar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: For myself personally and for those who were in Naim Vishaj's house in Beleg.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in Beleg did you see any other persons shooting at the various Serb forces you have described being in Beleg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were all the persons -- strike that. First of all, let's finish up one more question relating to the time-period when you were in the house of Naim. First of all, you said that the policemen told Naim to bring out all the men. Did the policemen speak in Serbian or some other language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Serbian. He spoke Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, were you able to understand him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I saw Naim when he said to the men, "Come outside." I heard Naim telling the men, "They want you to go all outside." I was in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that. What I'm asking you is: Did you in fact understand any of the Serbian that the police officer spoke?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I understood Naim when he addressed the men and told them that the police wanted them to go out. I didn't understand the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you mentioned a paralyzed lady that could not walk out of the house. Do you remember how that -- what that lady's name was or who she was, if not the name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I really don't remember her, but I know that she is the wife of Nezir Vishaj. I happened to spend time with her there, and I could see that she was really ill.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you have described paramilitaries, and you've described that they had on some sort of a green camouflage uniform. Now, did all of the paramilitaries that you've described wear the same uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Both camouflage uniforms and police uniforms, these two uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to focus on the camouflage uniforms, since you've already described the police uniforms. With respect to the camouflage uniforms, did you see any insignia, badges, markings, or other identifying features of those green camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I had no opportunity to look at these insignia; that was not on our minds at that time. We couldn't even look at them because we were scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you told us, at least in the statement, you identify that Mehmet Mazrekaj told you about his encounters with Zoran Djurisic and what Zoran Djurisic told him. Now, am I correct that you yourself did not have any personal contact or conversation with this individual he called Zoran Djurisic while at Beleg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I never had any contacts with him. I happened to see him while travelling on the bus during the war. He would get on the bus and ask us for identification papers; and while in Beleg, Zoran took Mehmet and placed him amidst us, and he beat him up as hard as he could. The children were screaming at this sight. Mehmet told the children, "Don't cry. You see, he used to be my pupil. I was his teacher in the past; and look at him now, he's beating me."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, am I correct that you did not know this individual's name prior to Mehmet Mazrekaj telling you this individual's name? That is to say, before this incident you had seen him asking for IDs on the road and letting -- and manning a check-point, but you had not known his identity, his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: You mean Zoran?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: As I said, only while on the bus during the war, he would get on and ask for identification papers. I heard people say that his name was Zoran. I had no other information about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That is enough. Now, with respect --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: And Mehmet also told us who he was when he was beating him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, with respect to what you told us here today, you said that the persons were checking people in the basement, and you indicated that they made people take off your clothes, that they were looking for money, et cetera. Were they -- did they also appear to be looking for anyone who had any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: There was no way they were looking for weapons. We were all civilians; children, women, young, elderly. They were not looking for weapons. They only wanted to take their valuables and money. When it was my turn to be searched, when I entered that area, they didn't even have to take off my clothes to search me, because I already prepared whatever I had on me, the money, the valuables, the jewellery, and took the rings out of my fingers, and gave them everything. I didn't wait for them to search me. I surrendered everything beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's actually what I wanted to ask you. Am I correct that in fact the persons in the basement with you did not even tell you to put your valuables anywhere, that they did not have any communication with you? You did this all of your own accord?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: No, no, no. They said, "Give us what you have from money and jewels -- jewellery." I didn't wait for them to come any near me. As soon as I entered the area, I took off every jewellery that I had on and the money, and I gave them everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's something that's not in your statement, so let me ask you: Who is it who told you to give them all your money and belongings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: The policemen who were there; those who were searching us. They were searching us one at a time, and they wanted to tell -- to take everything that we had. And this didn't happen only to me; it happened to everyone who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what language were these people speaking? Was it Serbian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Serbian, Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, you -- although you don't speak or read Serbian, you happened to understand what these policemen were saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I understood that, because when my turn came I saw that they had laid a sheet, and everyone who had been searched previously had put there everything from their jewellery and money. So I understood what was that about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in your statement at page 5, the fifth complete paragraph on that page, you say - and now I'm going to read that to you - talking about this incident where you put your 850 Deutschemarks and some jewellery on this white cloth, in reference to the two individuals who were there you say: "They did not say anything to me, and I was allowed to go out." So, again, I'm going to ask you: Why is it that now you say they told you in Serbian, "Give us all your belongings," when your signed and affirmed statement says they did not say anything to you? Which is the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: The truth is the following. My turn came later, and we asked the women that had been searched previously what happened to them and what they told them. And their reply was that they asked them for their money and jewellery. So when my turn came, I was so scared that I didn't wait for them to say anything; I just gave them everything I had, the money and jewellery, and left the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So a few minutes ago when you told me that they told you in Serbian to do that, you were not telling the truth, were you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point it's become --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm telling you the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please hold on for a moment. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour. At this point it's becoming argumentative. This witness has been very clear that she heard statements made in Serbia. She's following what everyone else was doing. Unless this is being held out she was being kind and giving a gift to the paramilitaries or the police who had her down in the basement and everyone else is giving their jewellery, this is becoming argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I disagree with that. If you read the statement where the sentence just referred to is set out, "They did not say anything to me," that's open to interpretation, so far as the order of events is concerned. But if you read the next sentence, you can't possibly claim that the matter is so clear that further cross-examination is inappropriate. Now, I don't want you to read that sentence out. And no doubt there are questions yet to come about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you may continue -- you've had an answer to the question anyway, so you can pose your next question, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, a couple of moments ago, you also told me that there was a white piece of cloth where other persons, who went before you, had placed their valuables. Now, in your sworn statement in the same paragraph that we've been discussing at page 5, it says, and I quote: "I was the first one to hand over my money and gold." How do you reconcile this difference in what you say in your statement and what you have told us under oath today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Listen, when my turn came, then I didn't wait for them to ask me to give away my jewellery or my money. And I saw the white cloth and then I put my money and the jewellery on that sheet, because I didn't know -- I didn't want them to harass me or to do anything to me. And eight years have passed since then, and I have been under trauma. So don't ask me to tell you exactly word for word what happened at that time to now. I'm just telling you what happened, what occurred then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ma'am, are you telling us we cannot rely upon the sworn testimony that you have given today orally, that it may not be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: No, sir. What I'm telling you is correct and true. It's something which happened to me, something which I witnessed, and I came here to testify to what I saw and what happened. I don't know and I don't want to tell lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In that case then, at the time that you put your belongings on the white sheet that was on the floor, there were no other belongings of no one else on that sheet at that time, were there? You were the first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I don't think I was the first. There were others before me, but what my point is that I gave my money and my jewellery myself before them asking me. But there were other women before me who were searched and who were asked to give away their money. When my turn came, I gave them my jewellery and my money. I didn't want them to search me bodily and ask me for them, because we were very scared. We didn't know what to do. We were lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I'm going to get an answer to my question, so I'll just move on. Now, with respect to the individuals that you said were still missing along with your husband, you have provided a list of, I don't know, perhaps a dozen individuals in your statement. Did you know all of these individuals personally? And I would caution you, don't tell us how you know them so as -- so that we can protect your identity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: These persons whose names are there, I knew them. They all disappeared along with my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you've already told us that your husband was not a member of the UCK. Do you know if any of the persons, I believe you identified -- I believe you stated that there were 60 such persons that are missing along with your husband, do you know if any of them were ever members of the UCK or assisted the UCK in any fashion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: The persons I knew, none of them was a member, none of them was. All of them were civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you know all 60, or did you only know these that are identified in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: No. I -- you see the names; Arif Mazrekaj, Jetmir Mazrekaj, Sahit Mazrekaj, Sundim Mazrekaj, Sahit Mazrekaj, Hajdar Mazrekaj. The names are there because I want to make sure I remember them, because eight years have passed since that time and I might forget.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. My question acknowledged that you had identified these individuals in your statement. My question was: Did you personally know all 60, because all 60 are not on this list; and with respect to all 60 did you personally know that they had never assisted the UCK in any fashion, or can you only say that about these that you have listed out that you actually know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: The ones whose names I have written on my statement I know; the others, no. I only know that they were taken away and are missing ever since.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, am I correct -- pardon me. Is your statement correct, when at page 7 you say: "The next morning at 9.00, two paramilitaries came and told us to get out. They said, 'Go to Albania. You have asked for NATO.'" . Is it correct that it was the paramilitaries who told you to leave Beleg, and not the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Because of my fright, I wasn't even looking at them to tell you who they were. I only know that they came at about 9.00 and told us to leave, to go to Albania, because we asked for NATO. And I said to them that I had my seven children, whom I had to take care of. Those were my primary concern. So I can't tell you for sure what they were. When I wrote the statement, maybe I thought that they were paramilitaries and I believed so. But at this moment, I cannot ascertain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be safe to say then that during your entire stay in Beleg, the situation was such that due to your fright and due to your obligations to your family, you did not pay close attention and differentiate between the various uniformed individuals walking around or in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: We couldn't distinguish between them, because we couldn't look up to them and see who they were, what they were wearing. I told you, I had my kids. The youngest was six months old, another was 3 years old, so I had to take care of them. There was no way we could look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only have about one more question, Your Honour. If I can finish that up, then I can finish this witness up before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The break won't be until quarter to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's right. I apologise. I forgot that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It wouldn't be licence for another series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It won't be, Your Honour. I only have the one area left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To finish up, ma'am, when we were talking about this individual, Zoran, earlier, you indicated that when you were riding the bus during the time of the war, is this in 1998 or 1999, first of all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: In 1998, sometimes we went to Peje. In 1999 -- I don't remember the year, the exact year. But I only know that he came into the bus and asked us for our permission, and I heard the man saying that his name was Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that was a -- this was a regular bus on the road, a passenger bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: The regular -- the regular bus in Kosova town. What do I know? I know that we used this bus for personal needs to go to the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how often did you see this individual Zoran get on the bus and examine persons' documents before letting the bus continue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I remember to have seen him twice. This is what I remember. Maybe one time, two times. I am not very sure, because that was not a matter of great interest to me. But, approximately, I think twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And these two times that you saw him, was that before or during the time when the OSCE mission was in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: During the time the OSCE was in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So it could be any time from October 1998 to March of 1999, you can't be -- can you be any more specific an that; if not, then please just tell me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I cannot be more specific than that. I didn't pay any attention with the war going on, with the war we had, with my kids, and everything we were experiencing, I cannot tell you for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, ma'am, for your testimony. I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, we have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mrs. K58.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Today, one of my colleagues asked you about your stay in Drenovac village. It's on page 21 in the transcript, lines 18 to 23. The question was whether you were aware that some Serb civilians from Locane had also escaped to Drenovac in March 1999. You answered that you knew nothing about that, because Drenovac is pretty far away from Locane. Is that correct? Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Yes, that's true that Drenoc is far from Lloqan. I don't know Lloqan very well to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that Locane is a village next door to Drenovac, and the first houses are no further away than 500 metres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: I don't know. Drenoc is a big village. My house is at the entrance to Drenoc, so I can't tell you for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What is the closest village to your home, if your house is the first as you enter the village? Is it the first when you are coming from Decani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Prilep is the first; Prilep, then comes Drenoc, then my house is closer to that area. And there is a road --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That would mean is that your home is closer to Locane village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: No, no. My house is at the entrance to Drenoc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Given that identification is supposed to be concealed for this witness, we're identifying exactly where she lives at this point. If we're going to continue on this, I mean the damage is already done in the first question. If we're going to continue this, I would ask that we do it in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say in the first question?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry the first question of this series in, regards to where the villages were and asking for specification of where she resides. When she answered the question, she's giving a pretty clear answer as to where she lives, which is in violation of concealment of her identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't mind, but I understood that she was there in 1999 in March. It's not where she lives now. I don't even where she lives now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that resolve the matter, Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: To respond to the question would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Visnjic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I live in the village of my husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't intend to pursue the matter further. The answer was quite clear. I would like to ask the witness something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, in the period while you stayed in Drenovac, whether there were any KLA in Drenovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: There was no KLA in Drenoc. When I was there, there was no one in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if in the same period, rather, do you know that in the same period the KLA -- if the KLA attacked either Serbs or Albanians or OSCE representatives on the territory of the village, of one of these villages, Donji Streoc, Dasinovac, Bagas [phoen], Rznic, Bandera, Gornja Luka, Istinic, Lumbarda, and Prilep. Do you know whether the KLA mounted any attacks in any of these places against Albanians, Serbs, or OSCE representatives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: No, no. This is the first time for me to hear that. I didn't know that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had my seven children to take care, and my concern was to feed them, to raise them, and so I didn't pay attention to these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Carter, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ms. K58, can you approximate how many women were being checked when the valuables were being laid on the white sheet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: There were many, but I cannot give you an exact number. If you asked me how many kids I had at that moment, I wouldn't be able to answer you, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that there was a large group of women in the meadow, and they were being brought in in smaller groups, such as four persons at a time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Carter --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I note no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]-- about 100 or more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I note no objection to that question, but I have to say it's pretty useless to the Chamber to receive evidence in re-examination through such leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, you indicated that you were the first person to lay -- to give over your valuables. Are you indicating that you are the first person in the entire group of women of the hundred that you're approximating, or were you the first person within the group of four in which you were brought into the basement?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivetic, I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the first of my group, but there were other groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question's been answered. Because I'd been looking for response and got none, I thought I had done well enough by intervening the last time. I agree it's not a as valuable an answer as it might have been if the question had been put another way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Ma'am, how many people were brought -- how many people, if any, were brought ahead of you to be checked in the basement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: We went there in groups, each group having four or five persons. Among my group, I was the first. And once I was there, I said I handed over my things and I left my friends, the friends of my group being checked at handing over their things. But in my group, once I heard, I submitted everything I had, and they beckoned me to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Madam, was yours the first group to be checked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There were other groups before our group, before me and my group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the checking place, can you please describe -- describe the white sheet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: When I entered there with my group, I was the first of my group. And I submitted everything I had, and then I left. I left behind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Madam, Madam --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop -- please listen to the question. You've told us a number of things about this. The question was very specific. Now, listen again to it, and please answer the particular question you're being asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When you arrived in the place in which you were checked, can you please describe the white sheet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K58
utterances.text: Yes. There was a normal-sized sheet. It was laid on the floor. And once we entered the basement, we surrendered what we had on us on the sheet. Because before we went there -- when my turn came, I saw the sheet other valuables being handed over by other women before us. So I didn't wait for them to ask me, then I gave them the gold coin I had and the valuables and surrendered them, put them on the white sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Carter, we'll have to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I left behind the friends of my group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll have to take the break there, and you can resume when we return.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, outside of indicating that the statement itself needs to be placed under seal and the Prosecution will provide a public redacted copy at an early time, I have no more questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: More precise on that by the end of the week?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: By Friday?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Madam Witness K58, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming before the Tribunal to give this evidence. When we adjourn in a moment, you will be free to leave. The Trial Chamber will now adjourn and resume at 20 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: After.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Neema, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I see Mr. Fila on his feet. I think he wanted to raise something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Fila, there's no interpretation coming through.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. They were on the wrong channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you start again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I will start again. The Defence counsel have conferred, and we have spoken to Mr. Hannis to inform him of our standpoint. On Friday, we have a problem with Dusan Loncar. The health problem is no longer there, but there is a problem of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we need to deal with this -- can we not leave this until we finish with our evidence today and then deal with it at that stage? No. Okay. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need Your Honour's authority. And it may take time; that's why I'm raising it now. All sides have agreed that Dusan Loncar can be heard tomorrow, tomorrow in the afternoon, say, and then we would have the entire time we need. We believe it is only Your Honour's authority that can bring this about. We have done all we could. Thank you. That's why I interrupted. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, my understanding was that the videolink could not be set up for tomorrow afternoon. That's the problem. This is a videolink witness in Belgrade, and the arrangements were made for Friday. Now, if that can be changed, I'm sure the Bench would happily agree to that, but I doubt if it can be. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's my understanding, Your Honour. We had some conversation with the registry last week, while the application was still pending, in light of the potential time problems we faced; and at that time I believe Mr. Haider advised me that there was a shortage of registry officers and technical people who could be in Belgrade on that date. And Friday seemed to be the date that we have. I'm willing to do it. I don't know if the witness is available or not to do it, if there was some change in the technical capability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I will make such inquiries as I can, but at this moment I'm not terribly optimistic about the outcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Neema, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEEMA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The next witness will be K74. This witness will be a Rule 92 ter witness/live witness. The Prosecution would like to make an application for more than 30 minutes of leading this witness, but we believe we won't be going more than one hour. And this witness's testimony is relevant to paragraphs 72(h), (i), and 75(g) of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give us a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's agreeable, Mrs. Neema, on the understanding that you'll obviously be doing your best to confine it, as far as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEEMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall have the witness now. Good morning, Witness K74, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which is now before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. And perhaps the registrar would adjust that microphone again so that we make sure that it conveys the sound adequately to this end. That looks better. You will now be asked questions by a number of counsel here, and the first to question you will be on behalf of the Prosecution, and that is Mrs. Neema. Mrs. Neema.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEEMA
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K74
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEEMA
utterances.text: Witness, before we proceed, I would like to remind you that you are giving testimony under a pseudonym; so throughout your testimony, you will be referred to as K74. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K74
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to speak into the microphone. We can't hear him very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Haider, there is a problem with sound again. Is there anything you can do with the microphone? Thank you very much. Mrs. Neema.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEEMA
utterances.text: Can we have identification sheet Exhibit P02513 in front of the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEEMA
utterances.text: Witness, could you please have a look at the document given to you and see if the information contained in there relates to you and is correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K74
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEEMA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would like to tender this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEEMA
utterances.text: -- this exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. NEEMA
